{{Short description|Law in algebraic number theory}}
In [[algebraic number theory]] '''Eisenstein's reciprocity law''' is a [[reciprocity law]] that extends the [[law of quadratic reciprocity]] and the [[cubic reciprocity law]] to residues of higher powers. It is one of the earliest and simplest of the higher reciprocity laws, and is a consequence of several later and stronger reciprocity laws such as the [[Artin reciprocity law]]. It was introduced by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Gotthold Eisenstein|last=Eisenstein|year=1850}}, though Jacobi had previously announced (without proof) a similar result for the special cases of 5th, 8th and 12th powers in 1839.<ref>Lemmermeyer, p. 392.</ref>

==Background and notation==

Let <math>m > 1</math> be an integer, and let <math>\mathcal{O}_m</math> be the [[ring of integers]] of the ''m''-th [[cyclotomic field]] <math>\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m),</math> where <math>\zeta_m=e^{2 \pi i\frac{1}{m}}</math> is a [[root of unity|primitive ''m''-th root of unity]].

The numbers <math>\zeta_m, \zeta_m^2,\dots\zeta_m^m=1</math> are [[unit (ring theory)|unit]]s in <math>\mathcal{O}_m.</math> (There are [[cyclotomic unit|other units]] as well.)

===Primary numbers===

A number <math>\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_m</math> is called '''primary'''<ref>Ireland & Rosen, ch. 14.2</ref><ref>Lemmermeyer, ch. 11.2, uses the term '''semi-primary.'''</ref> if it is not a [[unit (ring theory)|unit]], is [[relatively prime]] to <math>m</math>, and is congruent to a rational (i.e. in <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>) integer <math>(\!\bmod{(1-\zeta_m)^2}).</math>

The following lemma<ref>Ireland & Rosen, lemma in ch. 14.2 (first assertion only)</ref><ref>Lemmereyer, lemma 11.6</ref> shows that primary numbers in <math>\mathcal{O}_m</math> are analogous to positive integers in <math>\mathbb{Z}.</math>

Suppose that <math>\alpha, \beta\in\mathcal{O}_m</math> and that both <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are relatively prime to <math>m.</math> Then
*There is an integer <math>c</math> making <math>\zeta_m^c\alpha</math> primary. This integer is unique <math>(\!\bmod{m}).</math>
* if <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are primary then <math>\alpha\pm\beta</math> is primary, provided that <math>\alpha\pm\beta</math> is coprime with <math>m</math>.
* if <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are primary then <math>\alpha\beta</math> is primary.
* <math>\alpha^m</math> is primary.

<blockquote>
The significance of the <math>1-\zeta_m</math> that appears in the definition is most easily seen when <math>m=l</math> is a prime. In that case <math>l=(1-\zeta_l)(1-\zeta_l^2)\dots(1-\zeta_l^{l-1}).</math> Furthermore, the prime ideal <math>(l)</math> of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> is totally ramified in <math>\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_l)</math>
:<math>(l)=(1-\zeta_l)^{l-1},</math>
and the ideal <math>(1-\zeta_l)</math> is prime of degree 1.<ref>Ireland & Rosen, prop 13.2.7</ref><ref>Lemmermeyer, prop. 3.1</ref>

</blockquote>

===''m''-th power residue symbol===
{{main|Power residue symbol}}

For <math>\alpha, \beta\in\mathcal{O}_m,</math> the ''m''-th power residue symbol for <math>\mathcal{O}_m </math> is either zero or an ''m''-th root of unity:

:<math>
\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta }\right)_m
=
\begin{cases}
\zeta \mbox{ where }\zeta^m=1&\mbox{ if }\alpha\mbox{ and }\beta\mbox{ are relatively prime}\\
0 &\mbox{ otherwise}.\\
\end{cases}
</math>
It is the ''m''-th power version of the classical (quadratic, ''m'' = 2) [[Jacobi symbol]] (assuming <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are relatively prime):

* If <math> \eta\in\mathcal{O}_m </math> and <math>\alpha\equiv\eta^m\;(\bmod{\beta})</math> then <math>\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta }\right)_m = 1.</math>
* If <math> \left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta }\right)_m \neq1 </math> then <math>\alpha </math> is not an ''m''-th power <math>(\!\bmod{\beta}).</math>
* If <math> \left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta }\right)_m =1 </math> then <math>\alpha </math> may or may not be an ''m''-th power <math>(\!\bmod{\beta}).</math>

==Statement of the theorem==

Let <math>m\in\mathbb{Z}</math> be an odd prime and <math>a\in\mathbb{Z}</math> an integer [[relatively prime]] to <math>m.</math> Then

===First supplement===

:<math>
\left(\frac{\zeta_m}{a }\right)_m =
\zeta_m^{\frac{a^{m-1}-1}{m}}.
</math><ref name="Lemmermeyer, thm. 11.9" >Lemmermeyer, thm. 11.9</ref>

===Second supplement===

:<math>
\left(\frac{1-\zeta_m}{a }\right)_m =
\left(\frac{\zeta_m}{a }\right)_m^{\frac{m+1}{2}}.
</math><ref name="Lemmermeyer, thm. 11.9" />

===Eisenstein reciprocity===

Let <math>\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_m</math> be primary (and therefore relatively prime to <math>m</math>), and assume that <math>\alpha</math> is also relatively prime to <math>a</math>. Then<ref name="Lemmermeyer, thm. 11.9" /><ref>Ireland & Rosen, ch. 14 thm. 1</ref>

:<math>
\left(\frac{\alpha}{a }\right)_m =
\left(\frac{a}{\alpha }\right)_m. 
</math>

==Proof==

The theorem is a consequence of the [[Stickelberger relation]].<ref>Ireland & Rosen, ch. 14.5</ref><ref>Lemmermeyer, ch. 11.2</ref>

{{harvtxt|Weil|1975}} gives a historical discussion of some early reciprocity laws, including a proof of Eisenstein's law using Gauss and Jacobi sums that is based on Eisenstein's original proof.

==Generalization==
{{See also|Artin reciprocity}}
In 1922 [[Teiji Takagi|Takagi]] proved that if <math>K\supset\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_l)</math> is an arbitrary [[algebraic number field]] containing the <math>l</math>-th roots of unity for a prime <math>l</math>, then Eisenstein's law for <math>l</math>-th powers holds in <math>K.</math><ref>Lemmermeyer, ch. 11 notes</ref>

==Applications==

===First case of Fermat's Last Theorem===

Assume that <math>p</math> is an odd prime, that <math>x^p+y^p+z^p=0</math> for pairwise relatively prime integers (i.e. in <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>) <math>x,y,z</math> and that <math>p\nmid xyz.\;\;</math>

This is the [[first case of Fermat's Last Theorem]]. (The second case is when <math>p\mid xyz.\;</math>) Eisenstein reciprocity can be used to prove the following theorems

'''(Wieferich 1909)'''<ref>Lemmermeyer, ex. 11.33</ref><ref>Ireland & Rosen, th. 14.5</ref>  Under the above assumptions, <math>2^{p-1}\equiv 1 \; (\!\bmod{p^2}).</math>

:The only primes below 6.7×10<sup>15</sup> that satisfy this are 1093 and 3511. See [[Wieferich prime]]s for details and current records.

'''(Mirimanoff 1911)'''<ref>Lemmermeyer, ex. 11.37</ref> Under the above assumptions <math>3^{p-1}\equiv 1 \; (\!\bmod{p^2}).</math>

:Analogous results are true for all primes ≤ 113, but the proof does not use Eisenstein's law. See [[Wieferich prime#Connection with Fermat's Last Theorem]].

'''(Furtwängler 1912)'''<ref>Lemmermeyer, ex. 11.32</ref><ref>Ireland & Rosen, th. 14.6</ref>   Under the above assumptions, for every prime <math>r\mid x,\;\;r^{p-1}\equiv1 \; (\!\bmod{p^2}).</math>

'''(Furtwängler 1912)'''<ref>Lemmermeyer, ex. 11.36</ref> Under the above assumptions, for every prime <math>r\mid (x-y),\;\;r^{p-1}\equiv1 \; (\!\bmod{p^2}).</math>

'''(Vandiver)'''<ref>Ireland & Rosen, notes to ch. 14</ref> Under the above assumptions, if in addition <math>p>3,</math> then <math>x^p\equiv x,\; y^p\equiv y</math>, and <math>z^p\equiv z \; (\!\bmod{p^3}).</math>

===Powers mod most primes===

Eisenstein's law can be used to prove the following theorem (Trost, [[Nesmith Ankeny|Ankeny]], [[Claude Ambrose Rogers|Rogers]]).<ref>Ireland & Rosen, ch. 14.6, thm. 4. This is part of a more general theorem: Assume <math>x^n\equiv a\pmod{p}</math> for all but finitely many primes <math>p.</math> Then i) if <math>8\nmid n</math> then <math>a=b^n</math> but  ii) if <math>8|n</math> then <math>a=b^n</math> or <math>a=2^{\frac{n}{2}}b^n.</math></ref>  Suppose <math>a\in\mathbb{Z}</math> and that <math>l\nmid a</math> where <math>l</math> is an odd prime. If <math>x^l\equiv a \; (\!\bmod{p})</math> is solvable for all but finitely many primes <math>p</math>, then <math>a=b^l.</math>
